title: Runaway Process Detection (CPU Hog)
exclusions: Detects a sampled Linux process candidate whose cumulative `ps` CPU time increases by at least 240 CPU seconds in each of three consecutive approximately 300-second intervals. It does not measure instantaneous `top` utilization, prove continuous CPU execution between snapshots, prove that the process is defective or unauthorized, or establish host saturation, service impact, root cause, or remediation. It misses bursts shorter than the collection interval and processes absent from any required snapshot. The supplied process table does not provide a reliable process-start identifier, so PID reuse with the same command remains an identity limitation. CPU quota, cgroup, container-namespace, thread-level, scheduler, and hardware-topology semantics require separate context. Missing, late, malformed, truncated, or unparsed snapshots are telemetry failures rather than healthy results. No exception lookup, compliance assertion, regulatory attestation, or security attribution is part of the primary rule.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_runaway_process_cpu_15m` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch and triggered-alert history; the returned host, PID, command, user, three interval measurements, threshold, and sample timestamps; the four selected raw `sourcetype=ps` process-table snapshots; an independent source-health result; and the incident, workload-owner, or approved-test record. During validation or investigation, retain time-correlated on-host `ps` output and, where needed, `/proc/<pid>/stat` observations captured under an approved procedure. These artifacts demonstrate that indexed cumulative CPU-time samples met the configured candidate rule; they do not prove uninterrupted execution, complete collection, a stable process identity across PID reuse, production impact, or corrective action.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index with `Splunk_TA_nix` search-time knowledge, index four complete aligned `sourcetype=ps` table snapshots for `host=cpu-hog-positive` at exact five-minute sample times. In every snapshot include `PID=4242`, `COMMAND=cpu-burner`, `USER=svc_test`, and current `TIME` values `00:00:00`, `00:04:15`, `00:08:25`, and `00:12:50` in chronological order, plus at least one healthy process row. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds. Expect exactly one row for PID 4242 with `comparable_intervals=3`, `breach_intervals=3`, `min_process_cpu_pct=83.3`, `avg_process_cpu_pct=85.6`, `max_process_cpu_pct=88.3`, and `bucket_span_minutes=15`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In a separate fixed interval, index four equivalent snapshots for `host=cpu-hog-negative`, but give PID 5252 cumulative `TIME` values `00:00:00`, `00:04:15`, `00:06:40`, and `00:10:55`. The interval percentages are 85.0, 48.3, and 85.0; immediately before the final gate confirm `comparable_intervals=3` and `breach_intervals=2`, then expect zero final rows. Also verify zero rows when one snapshot is absent, when the PID or command differs in one snapshot, and when cumulative time decreases after a simulated process restart. A boundary fixture with 240 CPU seconds over 300 elapsed seconds must calculate 80.0 and count as a breach.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=ps` multi-line process-table snapshots produced by the `ps.sh` scripted event input supplied with the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). `os` and the 300-second input interval are explicit deployment choices. `multikv` expands each selected table. Required current Linux columns are `PID`, `TIME`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`; documented pre-8.7 field `CPUTIME` is accepted in place of `TIME`. `_time`, `_raw`, and `host` are Splunk metadata. Linux `ps` obtains process CPU accounting from procfs and renders `TIME` as cumulative CPU time in `[DD-]hh:mm:ss`; the SPL converts it to CPU seconds and computes deltas over actual sample elapsed seconds. The add-on's current `CPU` and backward-compatible `pctCPU` fields are not used because procps defines that percentage as CPU time divided by the process's entire elapsed lifetime, not utilization during the latest collection interval.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), using its `ps.sh` scripted event input and `sourcetype=ps` parsing and search-time knowledge. No premium Splunk app is required.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=ps host=* earliest=-25m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval snapshot_time=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| eventstats max(snapshot_time) as selected_snapshot_time by _time host
| where snapshot_time=selected_snapshot_time
| multikv
| eval process_id=trim(tostring(coalesce(PID,pid,process_id))), process_name=trim(coalesce(COMMAND,command,process_name,"(command unavailable)")), process_user=trim(coalesce(USER,user,process_user,"(user unavailable)")), cpu_time_text=trim(tostring(coalesce(TIME,CPUTIME,cputime)))
| where match(process_id,"^[0-9]+$") AND len(process_name)>0 AND match(cpu_time_text,"^(?:[0-9]+-)?[0-9]+:[0-5]?[0-9]:[0-5]?[0-9]$")
| rex field=cpu_time_text "^(?:(?<cpu_days>[0-9]+)-)?(?<cpu_hours>[0-9]+):(?<cpu_minutes>[0-5]?[0-9]):(?<cpu_seconds>[0-5]?[0-9])$"
| eval cpu_days=coalesce(tonumber(cpu_days),0), cpu_hours=tonumber(cpu_hours), cpu_minutes=tonumber(cpu_minutes), cpu_seconds=tonumber(cpu_seconds), cpu_time_seconds=(cpu_days*86400)+(cpu_hours*3600)+(cpu_minutes*60)+cpu_seconds
| stats max(cpu_time_seconds) as cpu_time_seconds latest(process_user) as process_user max(snapshot_time) as snapshot_time by _time host process_id process_name
| sort 0 host process_id process_name _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(_time) as prior_bucket last(snapshot_time) as prior_snapshot_time last(cpu_time_seconds) as prior_cpu_time_seconds by host process_id process_name
| eval bucket_gap_seconds=_time-prior_bucket, interval_seconds=snapshot_time-prior_snapshot_time, cpu_delta_seconds=cpu_time_seconds-prior_cpu_time_seconds
| where bucket_gap_seconds=300 AND interval_seconds>=240 AND interval_seconds<=360 AND cpu_delta_seconds>=0
| eval process_cpu_pct=(100*cpu_delta_seconds)/interval_seconds, is_breach=if(process_cpu_pct>=80.0,1,0)
| stats count as comparable_intervals sum(is_breach) as breach_intervals min(process_cpu_pct) as min_process_cpu_pct avg(process_cpu_pct) as avg_process_cpu_pct max(process_cpu_pct) as max_process_cpu_pct earliest(prior_bucket) as first_bucket latest(_time) as last_bucket earliest(prior_snapshot_time) as first_sample_time latest(snapshot_time) as last_sample_time latest(process_user) as process_user by host process_id process_name
| eval required_intervals=3, required_breach_intervals=3, threshold_process_cpu_pct=80.0, bucket_span_seconds=last_bucket-first_bucket, bucket_span_minutes=round(bucket_span_seconds/60,1), sample_span_minutes=round((last_sample_time-first_sample_time)/60,1), min_process_cpu_pct=round(min_process_cpu_pct,1), avg_process_cpu_pct=round(avg_process_cpu_pct,1), max_process_cpu_pct=round(max_process_cpu_pct,1)
| where comparable_intervals=required_intervals AND breach_intervals=required_breach_intervals AND bucket_span_seconds=900
| convert ctime(first_sample_time) ctime(last_sample_time)
| table first_sample_time last_sample_time host process_id process_name process_user min_process_cpu_pct avg_process_cpu_pct max_process_cpu_pct comparable_intervals breach_intervals bucket_span_minutes sample_span_minutes threshold_process_cpu_pct
| sort 0 -avg_process_cpu_pct host process_id
description: Reports one row when the same Linux host, numeric PID, and command appears in four consecutive selected five-minute `ps` snapshots and its cumulative process CPU time increases at a rate of at least 80.0 process-CPU percentage points in all three intervening intervals. The rule uses actual sample elapsed time, accepts intervals from 240 through 360 seconds, and requires consecutive five-minute bucket positions. In this convention one fully occupied logical CPU is 100%; a multithreaded process can exceed 100%. The result is a sustained high-CPU candidate, not proof of continuous execution or a runaway defect.
value: A single process that persistently consumes most of one logical CPU can lengthen queues, exhaust a CPU quota, increase latency, interfere with co-located work, and reveal a loop, failed retry policy, pathological input, or unexpectedly expensive batch job. Requiring three consecutive interval deltas avoids paging on one short sample while preserving the host, PID, command, user, and measured range needed to route the candidate to the workload owner and compare it with service latency, host capacity, deployments, and approved work.
implementation: Enable the add-on's supplied `ps.sh` scripted event input on Linux forwarders, route complete process tables to the deliberately selected `os` index, and collect every 300 seconds. Verify current `PID`, `TIME`, `COMMAND`, and `USER` fields after `multikv`. Save the SPL as `linux_runaway_process_cpu_15m`, schedule it every five minutes on five-minute boundaries, and alert only when one host/PID/command has three consecutive interval rates at or above 80.0%, where 100% means one logical CPU. Validate snapshot selection, cumulative-time parsing, restart behavior, collection freshness, and threshold tuning before paging.
visualization: Use a current-candidates table showing first/last sample, host, PID, command, user, minimum/average/maximum process-CPU percentage, interval count, threshold, and actual sample span. Add a drilldown line chart of per-interval CPU seconds and calculated percentage for the selected identity, a same-host chart of total CPU utilization, run-queue and service latency, and an independent collection-health panel showing last raw `ps` event and parsed row count. Label the unit `process CPU (%) — 100% = one logical CPU`; do not cap values at 100, add process percentages as if they were host utilization, render missing samples as zero, or label the result a confirmed runaway process.
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on classifies `sourcetype=ps` as Performance data, and CIM Performance defines generic `cpu_time` and `cpu_load_percent` fields. However, the model does not preserve this rule's complete process-table snapshots, PID/command identity, selected-snapshot timestamp, cumulative `TIME` parsing, and three consecutive source-specific deltas. No equivalent accelerated `tstats` search is claimed. An Endpoint process-start dataset or an average of lifetime `CPU`/`pctCPU` values is not equivalent to this interval-rate detector.

knownFalsePositives:
A returned row means the indexed cumulative CPU-time samples satisfied the rule. “False positive” here means that sustained consumption was expected, authorized, misidentified, or operationally harmless—not that the arithmetic fabricated CPU time.

1. **Approved performance, soak, or capacity tests** — `stress-ng`, benchmark harnesses, load generators, and resilience exercises may intentionally occupy one or more logical CPUs. Match the exact host, executable or command, test owner, change or test identifier, and bounded start/end time. Confirm cleanup rather than suppressing the tool permanently.

2. **Compilers, package builds, and CI workers** — GCC, Clang, Rust, Java, kernel, container-image, and package builds can legitimately keep compiler or linker processes above the policy for several intervals. Correlate the PID and command with the CI job, repository, runner, owner, expected parallelism, and queue duration; a new or orphaned build still warrants investigation.

3. **Batch analytics, compression, encryption, and media work** — Database maintenance, scientific jobs, report generation, backup compression, checksums, transcoding, and cryptographic processing are deliberately CPU-bound. Validate the scheduler job, input, service objective, host or cgroup allocation, and completion progress. An approved product name alone is not enough to suppress every invocation.

4. **Application startup, just-in-time compilation, cache rebuild, or recovery** — JVM and .NET compilation, search indexing, cache warm-up, replay after failover, and leader recovery can sustain CPU after a deployment or restart. Compare release, start time, deployment/change record, service latency, and expected warm-up duration. Repeated or lengthening warm-up may be the defect this rule should expose.

5. **Host oversubscription or cgroup quota context** — Eighty percent of one logical CPU can be harmless on a large idle host but severe for a container limited to one CPU; conversely, a multithreaded process can legitimately exceed 100%. Use host CPU count, quota and throttling metrics, run queue, steal time, and service objectives for severity. Do not reinterpret process percentage as percent of total host capacity.

6. **PID reuse, command truncation, or namespace ambiguity** — The supplied table lacks a reliable start tick. A process can exit and a replacement can receive the same PID and command, and host identity can differ from a container-visible PID. A CPU-time reset is rejected, but a coincidentally monotonic replacement can still bridge samples. Confirm `/proc/<pid>/stat` start time, executable, cgroup, namespace, and service history before claiming persistence.

7. **Duplicate, replayed, delayed, or malformed collection** — Duplicate input stanzas, table truncation, missing headers, absent search-time knowledge, clock changes, or late ingestion can distort identity and elapsed time. The SPL selects one raw snapshot per host and bucket and rejects intervals outside 240–360 seconds, but source-health review is still required.

**Safe suppression:** keep the base search and its results unchanged. Apply notification suppression only in a separate routing search or alert action using an owner-approved lookup keyed by exact `host`, stable command or executable identity, workload owner, `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, `reason`, `ticket`, and `approver`; add a scheduler job or deployment identifier when available. Suppress only when the alert interval falls within the bounded approval. Reject whole-fleet wildcards, PID-only entries, broad substrings such as `java` or `python`, missing owners, expired or open-ended windows, and permanent exemptions. Continue collection and review suppressed candidates for duration or behavior outside the approved plan.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement boundary

Install a currently supported release of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) on each Linux Universal Forwarder that will collect process tables, and deploy its parsing and search-time knowledge to the tiers required by the local Splunk topology. Check the current Splunkbase compatibility table before installation or upgrade; the listing warns that version 6.0 changed defaults and configuration files, so rehearse an upgrade outside production. Assign a Linux platform owner, workload owner, Splunk content owner, and response path. The search role needs read access to the deployment-selected operating-system index and permission to schedule the search, not unrestricted administration.

Understand the measurement before setting severity. Linux `/proc/<pid>/stat` records cumulative user-mode and kernel-mode CPU time in clock ticks, and `ps` reads procfs and renders cumulative process CPU as `TIME`. Procps documents `%CPU` as CPU time divided by the process's entire elapsed lifetime. That lifetime average is not the utilization since the preceding Splunk poll, so this rule deliberately ignores the add-on's current `CPU` and backward-compatible `pctCPU` percentage fields. It parses `TIME`, subtracts consecutive values, and divides the CPU-second delta by actual wall-clock sample elapsed seconds. A result of 80% means an average 0.8 logical CPU during that interval. On Linux a multithreaded process can accumulate more than one CPU second per wall second, so values above 100% are valid and must not be clamped.

The configured policy is at least 80.0 process-CPU percentage points in each of three consecutive intervals between four snapshots. With nominal five-minute collection, each breach requires at least 240 CPU seconds over 300 elapsed seconds and the first-to-last bucket span is 15 minutes. Eighty percent is a catalogue starting policy, not a threshold published by Linux, procps, or Splunk. Three sampled intervals do not prove continuous CPU execution between polls, and “runaway” is an investigation label rather than a diagnosis.

## Step 1 — Configure and verify complete process snapshots

Use the add-on-supplied `ps.sh` scripted event input. It is a scripted input, not a modular input, HEC poll, or Universal Forwarder app with Splunkbase ID 617. On a Universal Forwarder, copy only the exact installed `ps.sh` stanza from `Splunk_TA_nix/default/inputs.conf` into a controlled local configuration, as Splunk instructs; do not copy the entire default file. Preserve the installed script path and source type, then make the collection choices explicit. A five-minute local example is:

```ini
[script://./bin/ps.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 300
index = os
```

`interval=300` and `index=os` are this implementation's choices. If governance selects another index or interval, change the input, search bounds, allowed interval jitter, controls, and threshold interpretation together. Each execution emits a process table, so estimate event size and script overhead on hosts with large process counts before fleet rollout. Follow Splunk's current execution-rights and service-account guidance. Do not grant ad hoc privileges solely to make a dashboard green.

Inspect the winning input with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` on the collection node. Search `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-20m` and inspect `_raw`: each event must contain one aligned header and the expected process rows. Then run `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-20m | multikv | table _time host PID TIME CPUTIME CPU pctCPU COMMAND USER`. Splunk documents that add-on 8.7 and later uses raw Linux names including `TIME` and `CPU` while preserving `CPUTIME` and `pctCPU` for backward compatibility. Treat `TIME` as canonical and `CPUTIME` only as the documented legacy fallback.

Verify that all in-scope processes are present. A truncated table can omit the busiest process and turn no result into false reassurance. Compare raw row counts with an on-host snapshot such as `ps -eo user:32,pid,time,pcpu,lstart,comm,args --sort=pid` at a recorded instant, allowing for collection, forwarding, and indexing delay. Check service-account visibility, header alignment, command truncation, table event breaking, and local modifications. Do not demand an exact count after an unbounded delay because processes can start and exit between observations.

## Step 2 — Save, understand, and schedule the SPL

Save the supplied SPL as `linux_runaway_process_cpu_15m`. Schedule it every five minutes on five-minute boundaries with trigger condition “result count greater than zero.” The explicit `earliest=-25m@m latest=-5m@m` range selects four closed five-minute buckets and leaves the newest bucket out for ordinary collection latency. Measure fleet latency before changing that allowance. A schedule that is not aligned to five-minute boundaries invalidates the bucket assumptions and must be corrected or redesigned and retested.

Before table expansion, the search preserves each raw event timestamp, bins it, and selects only the latest raw snapshot for each host and bucket. Selecting before `multikv` prevents every process row from participating in snapshot selection and prevents two polls in one bucket from being mistaken for persistence. It also refuses to substitute an earlier parseable table when the latest selected event is malformed; that condition should surface in collection-health monitoring.

After `multikv`, the search normalizes the current and documented legacy field names, rejects headers and malformed CPU-time strings, and parses `[DD-]hh:mm:ss` into cumulative CPU seconds. The first `stats` produces at most one row for a host/PID/command in each selected snapshot. `sort 0` establishes chronological order, and `streamstats current=f window=1` attaches the prior bucket, actual snapshot time, and cumulative CPU value for the same identity. The delta must be nonnegative, the bucket gap must be exactly 300 seconds, and the actual snapshot interval must be between 240 and 360 seconds. Those checks reject missing bucket positions, obvious process-time resets, and intervals too distorted for the configured rate calculation.

The percentage is `100 × CPU-time delta ÷ actual elapsed seconds`. The search marks an interval at or above 80.0, then requires exactly three comparable intervals, all three breaches, and a 900-second first-to-last bucket span. It reports minimum, average, and maximum interval percentages rounded only after threshold evaluation. Do not average lifetime `CPU`, average host CPU, count raw rows over a day, or apply an 80% threshold without stating whether 100% means one logical CPU or the whole host.

The grouping identity is `host + PID + COMMAND`. This prevents unrelated processes on a host from being aggregated, but it is not a perfect process instance key. Current `ps.sh` output documented here does not provide procfs start ticks. A process can exit and a replacement can reuse the same PID and command; a decreasing `TIME` is rejected, but a replacement whose cumulative time happens to remain monotonic can still bridge samples. If a stable boot ID and `/proc/<pid>/stat` start tick are mandatory, build and validate a separate governed collector rather than inventing fields in this source.

## Step 3 — Validate arithmetic, persistence, and source behavior

Construct controls as complete, aligned table events matching an actual add-on snapshot. Testing only pre-extracted scalar fields skips `multikv` and is insufficient. Place the four positive snapshots at exact five-minute sample times with cumulative `TIME` values 0, 255, 505, and 770 seconds. The three deltas are 255, 250, and 265 CPU seconds over 300 seconds, yielding 85.0%, 83.3%, and 88.3%. Require exactly one final row and the field values stated in `controlTest`.

For the principal negative, use cumulative values 0, 255, 400, and 655 seconds. Confirm 85.0%, 48.3%, and 85.0%, three comparable intervals, two breach intervals before the last `where`, and zero final rows. Add these regression cases: omit the middle snapshot; change PID or command in one table; decrease cumulative time after a simulated restart; provide malformed `TIME`; place two raw tables in one host/bucket and verify only the later one is selected; use actual sample gaps of 239 and 361 seconds and verify rejection; and use exactly 240 CPU seconds over 300 elapsed seconds and verify the inclusive 80.0 boundary. Include a multithreaded case above 100% and verify that no normalization or cap is applied.

Validate on a disposable staging workload under an approved plan. Capture `ps -p <pid> -o pid,ppid,user,lstart,time,pcpu,comm,args` at each sample and compare the cumulative `TIME` progression with the indexed rows. For deeper identity checks, record field 22 (`starttime`) and fields 14 and 15 (`utime` and `stime`) from `/proc/<pid>/stat`, taking care that the parenthesized command can contain spaces and that tick values require the host's `_SC_CLK_TCK` conversion. Procfs is an independent host observation, not a field contract silently added to `sourcetype=ps`.

Do not compare the interval result directly with one `ps %CPU` value: procps defines that value over process lifetime. A contemporaneous interval-oriented tool can provide useful context, but different sampling windows, per-thread display modes, CPU-count conventions, and collection times can produce legitimate differences. Preserve exact timestamps and units. Separately verify alert scheduling and delivery, and build a source-health search that checks last raw event, snapshots per bucket, parseable row count, and host inventory coverage. A no-result detector cannot distinguish an idle fleet from a silent input.

This editorial review is documentation-only. It did not run `ps.sh`, index a fixture, execute the SPL in Splunk, validate alert delivery, or certify a Splunk platform/add-on/Linux combination. Keep `status=draft` until those controls pass in a representative environment and an appropriate SME approves the content.

## Step 4 — Tune the policy without changing its meaning

Start with 80.0% only after measuring expected process behavior by host role, CPU quota, workload class, and service objective. Because 100% means one logical CPU, the threshold is not 80% of total host capacity. On a 16-CPU host, one process at 80% represents about 5% of aggregate nominal CPU capacity; inside a one-CPU container quota, it can consume most of the allocation. Correlate host CPU count, cgroup quota and throttling, run queue, load, steal time, service latency, and application throughput before assigning urgency.

Tune persistence and threshold together. Raising the threshold reduces candidates but can miss quota-bound regressions. Requiring more intervals delays detection and increases the chance that short-lived processes disappear; requiring fewer intervals increases sensitivity to ordinary work. If collection changes from 300 seconds, revise the search window, bucket span, interval bounds, expected CPU-second deltas, fixtures, saved-search description, dashboard labels, and runbook. Do not merely edit `threshold_process_cpu_pct` while leaving evidence and tests with obsolete units.

Use separate routing policies for distinct host roles when necessary, while retaining one clearly defined base measurement. A CPU-bound build worker, low-latency trading service, database host, and constrained container have different consequences. Criticality `high` describes the catalogue's potential impact, not a mandatory page severity for every row. Page only when the sustained candidate and service context meet the organization's response criteria; otherwise create a ticket or owner review.

## Step 5 — Investigate, visualize, and preserve evidence

The runbook should first confirm collection freshness, retrieve the four selected raw events, and recalculate the three deltas. Verify host, PID, command, user, sample times, cumulative values, actual intervals, and threshold. On the host, confirm that the PID still exists and record its start time, executable, arguments, parent, threads, cgroup, namespace, CPU affinity, quota, and current cumulative CPU time. Compare with deployment, restart, batch scheduler, CI, maintenance, and approved-test records. Treat command strings and usernames as routing clues, not authorization evidence.

Correlate with total host CPU utilization, run queue, load average, steal time, throttling, pressure, service latency, error rate, throughput, and dependent-system health. High process CPU can be efficient useful work; low host utilization does not make a quota-bound process harmless, and high host utilization does not prove that this process caused the impact. For suspected loops or regressions, follow the application's approved diagnostic procedure for profiles, stack traces, traces, or dumps. Do not have the alert automatically kill, renice, restart, migrate, or profile a process. Those actions can interrupt useful work, lose evidence, expose sensitive data, or worsen an incident.

Visualize the candidate table and interval drilldown with explicit process-CPU units. Keep total-host percentage in a separate panel with a different label and scale. Show missing snapshots and parsing failures as unknown telemetry, not zero utilization. Restrict access to raw arguments and diagnostic artifacts because command lines, environment-derived text, tenant identifiers, and workload details may be sensitive.

Retain the saved-search and alert definitions, source input configuration, add-on version, selected tables, normalized result, source-health result, schedule and delivery history, host observations, owner decision, exception, and disposition under the approved operations retention policy. Evidence establishes what the sampled data and rule showed during the retained interval. It does not establish continuous monitoring outside that interval, process maliciousness, compliance, causation, or successful remediation.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot specific failure modes and suppress safely

* **No `ps` events** — Confirm that the supplied input is enabled, the add-on is installed on the collection node, scripts have supported execution rights, the effective stanza uses the intended index, forwarding is healthy, and the search role can read the index. Use `btool`, `splunkd.log`, and the add-on's troubleshooting process; there is no HEC token or vendor API for this input.
* **Raw tables exist but fields are null** — Verify the `ps` source type, add-on search-time knowledge, intact header and alignment, event breaking, and local transformations. Repair the source contract instead of inventing `cpu_pct` or searching arbitrary columns by position.
* **Only `CPUTIME` or `pctCPU` appears** — The documented backward-compatible extraction is active. The SPL accepts `CPUTIME`; it intentionally does not use `pctCPU` because that value is lifetime-based. Record the installed add-on version and test its exact output.
* **Intervals disappear** — Inspect missing buckets, actual snapshot gaps outside 240–360 seconds, PID or command changes, CPU-time resets, scheduler alignment, delayed ingestion, and clock adjustments. Do not weaken every guard until a row appears; determine which contract failed.
* **Values exceed 100%** — Confirm the process is multithreaded and compare CPU-time deltas with logical CPU count and cgroup limits. More than 100% is valid in the one-logical-CPU convention. Investigate only values impossible for the available CPUs or inconsistent with host evidence.
* **A busy process does not alert** — It may have been busy for fewer than three intervals, absent from one selected table, hidden by truncation or permissions, renamed, restarted, or high relative to a quota while below 80% of one CPU. Inspect the interval drilldown and source health before changing the threshold.
* **The row joins different process instances** — Check `/proc/<pid>/stat` start time, `lstart`, service restarts, namespaces, executable, and cgroup. The source identity is limited; preserve that caveat and adopt a separately tested start-identity collector if the risk is unacceptable.
* **Duplicate candidates or inflated volume** — Look for duplicate scripted-input stanzas, multiple collection layers, replay, more than one table per bucket, or command variations. Fix collection duplication rather than deduplicating all events by host and PID.

The primary SPL contains no exception lookup. For an approved test, build, batch, or warm-up window, preserve the base result and apply a separately governed routing exception with exact workload identity, owner, ticket, approver, and bounded start and end epochs. Review matches during suppression and expire the entry automatically. Never suppress every process on a host, every invocation of a runtime name, all root-owned work, or a PID indefinitely.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for one program using most of a processor again and again, instead of reacting to a brief burst. That gives the team time to check whether it is useful work or a problem before other work slows down.
